scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Giddha originates from an ancient ring dance that was dominant in Punjab.
It has been practiced continuously through the Partition of India in 1947, which divided Punjab between India and Pakistan.
Since then, Giddha has been consolidated and promoted as an iconic expression of Punjabi culture on both sides of the border.
on_screen: Map: India, Pakistan · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Giddha is performed mainly at festive and social occasions like weddings.
It serves as a medium for women to narrate stories of their lives, including sexuality, through song and movement.
It is a celebration of Punjabi femininity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Giddha is accompanied by rhythmic clapping and folk songs performed by elder women.
Instruments like the dhol drum are not typically used, though sometimes small percussion such as dholak or spoon clapping may be present.
Listen for the Clapping, Occasional dholak or spoon percussion.
A lively folk vocal call-and-response led by elder women, accompanied by rhythmic hand clapping and occasional light percussion, creating an energetic and communal sound.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women traditionally wear brightly colored salwar kameez or ghagra, accessorized with folk jewelry.
Hair is styled in two braids with folk ornaments and a tikka on the forehead.
The dance is performed in social and festive settings, especially weddings.
